screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn what variables are in Arduino sketches, why choosing the right data type matters, and how operators let you compute and compare values. Variables are named containers that hold values while your program runs, and in Arduino’s C/C++ heritage you must declare each variable’s type so the compiler knows how much memory to allocate and what operations are valid. You will see examples such as integer and floating point declarations, constants that make code easier to maintain, and operators for math and logic. We will look closely at integer division and modulo, and at overflow risks that happen when a value grows past a type’s limit. Each section includes a concrete code example and a short exercise so you can practice selecting types and predicting outputs. By the end you will be able to declare variables for sensors, choose types for ranges you expect, and reason about when arithmetic yields integer or decimal results. Think about a sensor you might read: what type and size would you choose and why?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In these objectives you will find four practical skills to build. First, you will declare and use variables in an Arduino sketch so that your code stores and updates sensor readings and state. For example, declaring a variable for a potentiometer reading lets you sample and process input over time. Second, you will choose appropriate data types for integers, decimals, characters, booleans, and large numbers. Selecting the right type helps avoid overflow and saves memory on limited boards. Third, you will apply arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators to perform calculations and make decisions, such as comparing a sensor value to a threshold and combining conditions with logical AND. Fourth, you will understand type conversion and overflow risks: know when integer math truncates decimals and how exceeding a type’s range wraps values. Each objective is framed for practical use on boards like the Arduino Uno and includes short examples so you can practice making safe choices. As you work through the lesson, check your understanding by predicting outputs and selecting types for concrete scenarios.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: This slide outlines practice tasks and an assessment idea to reinforce the objectives. You will write a small sketch that declares variables such as potentiometerValue, mappedValue, and threshold. Use arithmetic to average three readings and print the result to the Serial Monitor. Practicing both coding and prediction trains both implementation and reasoning. Another common trap is choosing an int where a sensor value could exceed the range; the assessment asks you to justify type choices. Work through the exercise, then check your predictions against the Serial output to confirm your understanding.

screens.title: What is a variable?
screens.narratorSegment: A variable is a named container that stores a value while your program runs. In Arduino code you declare a variable with a specific type so the compiler knows how many bytes to reserve and which operations are allowed. For example, declaring an integer variable for a sensor reading tells the compiler to allocate two bytes on the Arduino Uno. Variables can be initialized when declared or assigned later, and their value can change during execution. A concrete example is declaring an integer named sensorValue, reading an analog input into it, and then using that value to make decisions or send to the Serial Monitor. A common misconception is to think variables are labels rather than storage; if you only name a value without reserving storage the program cannot hold changing data across iterations. Another pitfall is assuming a variable keeps values between program restarts; it only holds data while the sketch runs unless saved to persistent storage. Takeaway: variables let your sketch remember state and intermediate results. Question to reflect on: what two values would you store to debounce a button and why?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Variables store data at runtime; declaring a type reserves memory and defines allowed operations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is a variable?
Definition & Why it matters

Variables let your sketch hold sensor values, counters, and state that change over time. Declaring a type reserves appropriate memory and enforces valid operations.

Concrete example
int sensorValue = 0;
sensorValue = analogRead(A0);
Common misconception
Variables are permanent storage. They are not preserved across power cycles unless explicitly saved to persistent memory.
Pro tip
Give descriptive names and initialize variables to avoid undefined values on first use.
Visual: variable role
Name
A readable identifier, e.g., sensorValue.
Type
Declares storage size and valid operations.
Value
The current data stored and used by the program.
Key Takeaway

Declare variables with a suitable type so code stores and updates necessary values reliably.

screens.title: Common integer and byte types
screens.narratorSegment: Arduino offers several integer types with different sizes and ranges. The most common is int. On an Arduino Uno, an int uses two bytes and holds values from minus thirty two thousand seven hundred sixty eight to thirty two thousand seven hundred sixty seven. If your values may exceed that range, use long, which is four bytes and supports much larger positive and negative numbers. For small positive-only values, byte uses a single byte and holds zero to two hundred fifty five; it’s useful for pin numbers, small counters, or compact data buffers. A concrete example: use byte to store an LED pin number, int to hold a typical sensor ADC reading, and long for a millisecond timestamp that may grow large. A misconception is assuming int is always four bytes; size depends on the board and toolchain. Another mistake is overusing long by default, which uses more memory than necessary on resource-limited boards. Takeaway: match the type to the expected range and memory constraints. Ask yourself: for a counter that increments every millisecond, which type will avoid overflow during a long run?

keyIdea.title: Type selection
keyIdea.text: Pick int for typical signed integers, long for larger ranges, and byte for small nonnegative values to conserve memory.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Integer Types
Type comparison
int
2 bytes on Uno; range −32,768 to 32,767. Good for typical sensor values and counters within that range.
long
4 bytes; used when values must exceed int range, such as millisecond timestamps over long runtimes.
byte
1 byte; holds 0–255. Ideal for small positive indices, pin numbers, and compact storage.
Concrete scenarios
  • LED pin: byte ledPin = 13; small and nonnegative.
  • ADC reading: int sensorValue = analogRead(A0); stays within int range.
  • Uptime in ms: long uptime = millis(); may exceed int and needs long.
Key Takeaway

Match integer type to expected range to prevent overflow and conserve memory.

screens.title: Floating point and decimal numbers
screens.narratorSegment: Floating point numbers represent values with fractional parts and are declared with the float type in Arduino. A float uses four bytes and can represent decimals, which is useful for temperature readings or calculations that require fractional precision. However, floating point math is slower and less precise than integer math on small microcontrollers; some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly. For example, storing 23.5 in a float will work, but be mindful of rounding when comparing floats for equality. A concrete example: calculating an averaged temperature using floats gives a fractional result you can print with higher resolution. A common misconception is assuming floats are infinitely precise; instead, use a tolerance when comparing floats or prefer scaled integers for fixed precision if performance and exactness matter. Takeaway: use floats when you need decimals, but weigh precision and speed trade-offs on resource-limited devices. How would you store values in hundredths without using floats? Floating point and decimal numbers means use float for fractional values but be aware of precision limits and slower arithmetic compared to integers.. In practical terms, float: fractional values, precision, and trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Float use
keyIdea.text: Use float for fractional values but be aware of precision limits and slower arithmetic compared to integers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Floating point
When to use float

Floats store fractional values like voltage, temperature, or averaged readings. Use them when fractional precision is required for display or control decisions.

Code example
float temperature = 23.5;
float average = (a + b + c) / 3.0;
Misconception
Floats are exact. In reality they are approximations and require tolerance checks for equality.
Alternative: scaled integers
If you need exact fixed precision and faster math, store values scaled by a factor, for example store hundredths as integers and divide when printing.
Example scenario
To keep two decimal places for currency-like values, store cents in an int instead of using float to avoid subtle rounding errors.
Key Takeaway

Use float for decimals when convenient, but prefer scaled integers for exactness and speed when appropriate.

screens.title: Boolean and character types
screens.narratorSegment: Boolean and character types are simple but important. Use bool or boolean to store true or false values such as whether a button is pressed or a device is active. This simplifies conditional checks and keeps code readable. Use char to store a single character, for example a grade letter or a small protocol marker. Note that char occupies one byte; on Arduino char may be signed or unsigned depending on the implementation, so treat numeric operations with care. A concrete example: declare bool isRunning = true to gate behavior inside loop iterations, or char grade = 'A' when you need a single character label. A common misconception is to use strings where a char would suffice; strings allocate more memory and are slower. Another trap is assuming boolean arithmetic behaves like integers in all contexts; explicit comparisons clarify intent. Takeaway: use bool for flags and char for single-character data to keep memory usage low and intent clear. Consider: would you store LED states for many pins as individual booleans or as a packed bitfield? Boolean and character types means use bool for binary state and char for single characters; both are memory-light and expressive when used appropriately.. In practical terms, bool / boolean and char for flags and single characters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Bool & Char
bool / boolean
Store true/false values like buttonPressed or isRunning. Useful for conditionals and state machines.
Example
bool isRunning = true;
if (isRunning) {
  // do work
}
char
Holds a single character. Use for concise labels or protocol markers where full strings are unnecessary.
Example
char grade = 'A';
Serial.print(grade);
Misconceptions & Tips
  • Don’t use full strings when a char or boolean suffices; memory matters on microcontrollers.
  • Be explicit in comparisons to avoid accidental integer promotion or ambiguous truthiness.
Key Takeaway

Use bool for flags and char for single characters to keep code clear and memory use small.

screens.title: Constants and #define
screens.narratorSegment: Constants are values that do not change during program execution and declaring them improves code clarity and maintainability. In Arduino you can declare constants with the const keyword, for example declaring a pin number or reference voltage, and you can also use the preprocessor directive to define symbolic names. Using constants avoids magic numbers scattered throughout your code, which makes adjustments easier when hardware changes. A concrete example is setting a constant button pin and then using that symbolic name across setup and loop; changing the pin later requires a single edit. A misconception is thinking constants cost zero memory; some constants are stored in R A M unless declared with specific attributes or used in ways the compiler can optimize. Another practical tip is to use uppercase naming for constants to signal intent. Takeaway: prefer const for typed constants and use preprocessor defines for conditional compilation or compile-time flags. Reflect: which values in your sketch would become clearer as constants? Constants and #define means use const and #define to centralize fixed values, improving readability and simplifying future hardware changes.. In practical terms, why constants help maintainability and how to declare them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Constants matter

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Constants
const keyword
Typed constant that the compiler can use for checks and optimizations.
const int BUTTON_PIN = 2;
const float VOLTAGE_REF = 5.0;
#define
Preprocessor symbol replaced at compile time. Useful for compile-time flags and conditional compilation.
#define LED_PIN 13
// used by preprocessor
Why this matters
  • Single source of truth for hardware constants.
  • Easier refactoring when pins or calibration values change.
  • Better readability for other developers and your future self.
Key Takeaway

Declare fixed values as constants to reduce errors and simplify updates when hardware or calibration changes.

screens.title: Arithmetic operators
screens.narratorSegment: Arithmetic operators let you compute values and transform sensor readings. The basic set includes addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulo which gives the remainder of division. Use addition and subtraction for offsets and calibration, multiplication and division for scaling or mapping ranges, and modulo for wrapping counters or checking divisibility. A concrete example is mapping three readings to an average: add them and divide by three. Remember the important caveat: if you divide two integers, the result will be an integer with the fractional part removed. For example, dividing five by two using integer operands yields two. To get a decimal result, ensure at least one operand is a float. Modulo is useful for detecting events at intervals, such as running code every tenth loop when a counter modulo ten equals zero. A common misconception is to expect modulo to produce negative results consistently; behavior depends on sign and implementation, so prefer positive counters for periodic checks. Takeaway: use operators deliberately and check operand types to control integer versus floating point results. What expression would you use to constrain a counter to 0–255?

keyIdea.title: Arithmetic rules
keyIdea.text: Operators compute results but operand types determine integer vs decimal outcomes; use modulo for periodic behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Arithmetic Operators
Operators list
  • + addition for sums and offsets
  • - subtraction for differences and correction
  • * multiplication for scaling
  • / division; watch integer division vs float
  • % modulo for remainders and periodic checks
Examples
int sum = a + b + c;
float avg = (a + b + c) / 3.0;
int wrap = counter % 256; // keeps values 0–255
Common pitfall
Integer division discards decimals. Make one operand a float to get a decimal result.
Key Takeaway

Control types of operands to ensure the intended numeric result; use modulo for wrapping and periodic checks.

screens.title: Comparison and logical operators
screens.narratorSegment: Comparison operators determine relationships between values and return true or false; logical operators combine those boolean results to form complex conditions. For comparisons use equal, not equal, greater than, less than, and their inclusive variants to check values. Then use logical AND and OR to require multiple conditions or accept alternatives, and NOT to invert a boolean. A concrete scenario: check if a temperature reading is between two bounds using a lower-than comparison AND an upper-than comparison. Another example: skip an action if a sensor is out of range using the NOT operator. A common mistake is using a single equals sign instead of the equality comparison; in C-style languages, a single equals assigns a value rather than comparing, and that causes logical bugs. Also avoid chaining comparisons as in some other languages; write explicit comparisons combined with logical operators. Takeaway: comparisons produce boolean results; combine them with logical operators to form clear conditions. Try: how would you express a condition that a reading is greater than ten and the device is enabled? Comparison and logical operators means use comparison operators to produce boolean results and logical operators to combine conditions clearly and safely.. In practical terms, ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= and &&, ||, ! for decisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decision logic
keyIdea.text: Use comparison operators to produce boolean results and logical operators to combine conditions clearly and safely.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Comparison & Logic
Comparison operators
  • == equal to
  • != not equal to
  • < > <= >= for ordering
if (temp > 20) { /* warm */ }
if (mode == 1) { /* mode A */ }
Logical operators
Combine booleans with AND, OR, and NOT to express compound conditions.
if ((temp > 10) && (temp < 30)) { /* in range */ }
if (!buttonPressed) { /* not pressed */ }
Pitfalls
  • Don't use assignment where you mean comparison; it changes the variable instead of testing it.
  • Be explicit with parentheses when combining many conditions to avoid ambiguous precedence.
Key Takeaway

Write clear comparisons and combine them with logical operators to express conditions safely and readably.

screens.title: Integer division and modulo
screens.narratorSegment: Integer division and modulo often surprise learners. When both operands are integers in C-style languages, division yields an integer result by discarding the fractional part. For example, dividing seven by two with integer operands yields three in many languages, but on Arduino the behavior is that the fractional part is removed. If you want a decimal result, make at least one operand a float by including a decimal or casting. Modulo returns the remainder after integer division; it is handy for periodic actions, splitting cycles, or checking divisibility. For instance, a counter modulo ten equals zero every tenth iteration, which you can use to trigger a periodic task. A common misconception is expecting modulo to behave like floating remainder; modulo works on integers and negative operands can produce implementation-dependent results. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Division & Modulo
Integer division
When both operands are integers, the result is truncated to an integer. To get decimals, use a float operand or cast.
int r = 7 / 2; // r becomes 3
float f = 7.0 / 2; // f becomes 3.5
Modulo
Returns remainder. Useful for wrapping counters and timed events.
int r = 10 % 3; // r is 1
if (counter % 10 == 0) { /* every tenth loop */ }
Pitfall
Modulo with negative numbers can be surprising; prefer nonnegative counters for periodic checks.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Type conversion and overflow
screens.narratorSegment: Type conversion happens when operations mix types or when you assign a value to a variable with a different type. Conversions may be implicit or explicit; implicit conversions follow language rules and can truncate or change values unexpectedly. For example, assigning a float to an int truncates the fractional part. Overflow occurs when a value exceeds the storage range of its type — on an Arduino Uno, adding one to an int at its maximum wraps the value to the negative end. This wrapping can silently corrupt counters or sensor readings. A concrete example: if an int holds 32,767 and you increment it, it becomes −32,768, which may break logic that expects monotonic increases. Avoid overflow by choosing larger types like long when the expected range exceeds int, or by checking ranges before arithmetic. Another mitigation is modular arithmetic when wrapping is intentional. Takeaway: be deliberate about conversions and type ranges; always reason about the maximum values your variables may hold. Question: which type would you choose for a millisecond uptime counter expected to run more than one hour? Type conversion and overflow means implicit conversions can truncate data and overflow causes wrap-around; choose types and checks to prevent silent bugs.. In practical terms, how values change type and what causes wrapping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Implicit conversion
Mixing types in expressions may convert operands automatically, possibly losing precision or changing sign.
int x = (int) someFloat; // fractional part truncated
Overflow example
An int at its max plus one wraps to the minimum negative value on typical Arduino Uno settings.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Practice Sketch
Sketch pattern
int reading1 = 0;
int reading2 = 0;
int reading3 = 0;
float average = 0.0;
int threshold = 500;

// read three values
reading1 = analogRead(A0);
reading2 = analogRead(A1);
reading3 = analogRead(A2);

// compute average as float
average = (reading1 + reading2 + reading3) / 3.0;

// compare to threshold
if (average > threshold) {
  // take action
}

Serial.println(average);

  • Use float division to keep fractional average.

  • Print results to inspect and verify behavior.
Common mistake
Using integer division reduces the average to an integer; make one operand a float to preserve decimals.

Run the sketch and compare predicted results to actual output to learn how type choices affect calculations.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn what variables are in Arduino sketches, why choosing the right data type matters, and how operators let you compute and compare values. Variables are named containers that hold values while your program runs, and in Arduino’s C/C++ heritage you must declare each variable’s type so the compiler knows how much memory to allocate and what operations are valid. You will see examples such as integer and floating point declarations, constants that make code easier to maintain, and operators for math and logic. We will look closely at integer division and modulo, and at overflow risks that happen when a value grows past a type’s limit. Each section includes a concrete code example and a short exercise so you can practice selecting types and predicting outputs. By the end you will be able to declare variables for sensors, choose types for ranges you expect, and reason about when arithmetic yields integer or decimal results. Think about a sensor you might read: what type and size would you choose and why?

In these objectives you will find four practical skills to build. First, you will declare and use variables in an Arduino sketch so that your code stores and updates sensor readings and state. For example, declaring a variable for a potentiometer reading lets you sample and process input over time. Second, you will choose appropriate data types for integers, decimals, characters, booleans, and large numbers. Selecting the right type helps avoid overflow and saves memory on limited boards. Third, you will apply arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators to perform calculations and make decisions, such as comparing a sensor value to a threshold and combining conditions with logical AND. Fourth, you will understand type conversion and overflow risks: know when integer math truncates decimals and how exceeding a type’s range wraps values. Each objective is framed for practical use on boards like the Arduino Uno and includes short examples so you can practice making safe choices. As you work through the lesson, check your understanding by predicting outputs and selecting types for concrete scenarios.

This slide outlines practice tasks and an assessment idea to reinforce the objectives. You will write a small sketch that declares variables such as potentiometerValue, mappedValue, and threshold. Use arithmetic to average three readings and print the result to the Serial Monitor. This exercise forces you to pick types and to observe integer versus decimal behavior. For assessment, you will predict outputs of expressions such as integer division and modulo, and a logical expression combining comparisons. Practicing both coding and prediction trains both implementation and reasoning. A common mistake is assuming division always produces decimals; you will test that and learn how to force a decimal result when needed. Another common trap is choosing an int where a sensor value could exceed the range; the assessment asks you to justify type choices. Work through the exercise, then check your predictions against the Serial output to confirm your understanding.

A variable is a named container that stores a value while your program runs. In Arduino code you declare a variable with a specific type so the compiler knows how many bytes to reserve and which operations are allowed. For example, declaring an integer variable for a sensor reading tells the compiler to allocate two bytes on the Arduino Uno. Variables can be initialized when declared or assigned later, and their value can change during execution. A concrete example is declaring an integer named sensorValue, reading an analog input into it, and then using that value to make decisions or send to the Serial Monitor. A common misconception is to think variables are labels rather than storage; if you only name a value without reserving storage the program cannot hold changing data across iterations. Another pitfall is assuming a variable keeps values between program restarts; it only holds data while the sketch runs unless saved to persistent storage. Takeaway: variables let your sketch remember state and intermediate results. Question to reflect on: what two values would you store to debounce a button and why?

Arduino offers several integer types with different sizes and ranges. The most common is int. On an Arduino Uno, an int uses two bytes and holds values from minus thirty two thousand seven hundred sixty eight to thirty two thousand seven hundred sixty seven. If your values may exceed that range, use long, which is four bytes and supports much larger positive and negative numbers. For small positive-only values, byte uses a single byte and holds zero to two hundred fifty five; it’s useful for pin numbers, small counters, or compact data buffers. A concrete example: use byte to store an LED pin number, int to hold a typical sensor ADC reading, and long for a millisecond timestamp that may grow large. A misconception is assuming int is always four bytes; size depends on the board and toolchain. Another mistake is overusing long by default, which uses more memory than necessary on resource-limited boards. Takeaway: match the type to the expected range and memory constraints. Ask yourself: for a counter that increments every millisecond, which type will avoid overflow during a long run?

Floating point numbers represent values with fractional parts and are declared with the float type in Arduino. A float uses four bytes and can represent decimals, which is useful for temperature readings or calculations that require fractional precision. However, floating point math is slower and less precise than integer math on small microcontrollers; some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly. For example, storing 23.5 in a float will work, but be mindful of rounding when comparing floats for equality. A concrete example: calculating an averaged temperature using floats gives a fractional result you can print with higher resolution. A common misconception is assuming floats are infinitely precise; instead, use a tolerance when comparing floats or prefer scaled integers for fixed precision if performance and exactness matter. Takeaway: use floats when you need decimals, but weigh precision and speed trade-offs on resource-limited devices. How would you store values in hundredths without using floats? Floating point and decimal numbers means use float for fractional values but be aware of precision limits and slower arithmetic compared to integers.. In practical terms, float: fractional values, precision, and trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Boolean and character types are simple but important. Use bool or boolean to store true or false values such as whether a button is pressed or a device is active. This simplifies conditional checks and keeps code readable. Use char to store a single character, for example a grade letter or a small protocol marker. Note that char occupies one byte; on Arduino char may be signed or unsigned depending on the implementation, so treat numeric operations with care. A concrete example: declare bool isRunning = true to gate behavior inside loop iterations, or char grade = 'A' when you need a single character label. A common misconception is to use strings where a char would suffice; strings allocate more memory and are slower. Another trap is assuming boolean arithmetic behaves like integers in all contexts; explicit comparisons clarify intent. Takeaway: use bool for flags and char for single-character data to keep memory usage low and intent clear. Consider: would you store LED states for many pins as individual booleans or as a packed bitfield? Constants are values that do not change during program execution and declaring them improves code clarity and maintainability. In Arduino you can declare constants with the const keyword, for example declaring a pin number or reference voltage, and you can also use the preprocessor directive to define symbolic names. Using constants avoids magic numbers scattered throughout your code, which makes adjustments easier when hardware changes. A concrete example is setting a constant button pin and then using that symbolic name across setup and loop; changing the pin later requires a single edit. Arithmetic operators let you compute values and transform sensor readings. The basic set includes addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulo which gives the remainder of division.
